qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture four. Replication. This is how copies of the data keep a system running, and what can go wrong with them.
Six hundred requests a second, on one big machine or on three small ones.
600 requests a second, on one machine or three.
Then the big machine crashes, and nothing is served.
The big machine crashes: nothing is served.
When one small machine crashes, the other two still serve four hundred.
A small one crashes: 400 are still served.
So scaling out survives failures.
Scaling out survives failures.
In replication, every node keeps a full copy of the data.
Replication: every node keeps a full copy.
In partitioning, each node keeps only a piece. That comes in the next lecture.
Partitioning: each node keeps a piece.
When a node fails, replication still has two copies of B, and partitioning has none.
When a node fails, the copies carry on.
A client changes its profile picture three times. Every write goes to the leader.
Every write goes to the leader.
The leader stores each one in a log, and sends it on, in order, to the followers.
It sends each change on, in order, as a log.
Reads can go to any node, but writes only go to the leader.
Reads can go to any node, writes only to the leader.
The leader stores a write in five milliseconds.
The leader stores the write in 5 ms.
The followers confirm at thirty-five and ninety-five milliseconds.
Followers confirm at 35 and 95 ms.
The leader can answer at once, or wait for one follower, or wait for both.
Answer at once, or wait for the followers.
If the leader crashes, answering at once loses the write. Waiting keeps it, but is slower.
If the leader then crashes, only waiting keeps the write.
A new follower needs a copy of the data.
A new follower needs a copy.
So we take a snapshot of the leader.
Take a snapshot of the leader.
Writes keep coming while the snapshot is copied.
Writes keep coming while it copies.
The follower then asks for every change since entry five.
It asks for every change since.
It applies them, and has caught up. Writes never paused.
Caught up: no pause in writes.
The leader has written twenty changes, but the followers lag behind.
The leader wrote 20 changes; followers lag.
Then the leader crashes. Which follower should take over?
The leader crashes. Which follower takes over?
Promoting A would lose five changes, B two, and C four. The most up to date wins.
Best: the most up-to-date follower.
So B takes over and becomes the leader.
B takes over.
The last two changes, which no follower had, are lost.
The 2 changes no follower had are lost.
Here A is the leader.
A is the leader.
Then A is cut off. It is still running, but B and C think it died.
A is cut off; B and C think it died.
So B is promoted. But A does not know, so it still thinks it leads.
B is promoted, yet A still leads.
Now two clients write to seat twelve. Ann goes to A, and Bo goes to B.
Both take a write for seat 12.
The network heals, and the two histories disagree. That is split brain.
Split brain: two histories disagree.
You post a comment, and it goes to the leader.
You post a comment to the leader.
You reload, but a follower that lags still shows three comments.
Reload: a follower that lags still shows 3.
Your own comment seems to be gone.
Your comment seems to be gone.
The fix is to read your own recent posts from the leader.
Fix: read your own recent posts from the leader.
You refresh, and replica A says seven likes.
Refresh: replica A says 7.
You refresh again, and replica B says six. Time ran backwards.
B says 6: time ran backwards.
The fix is to keep each user on one replica.
Fix: keep each user on one replica.
Then their view only moves forward.
Their view only moves forward.
Copies keep the system up. One leader takes the writes, and passes them to the followers.
Waiting for followers is safer, but slower.
When the leader crashes, promote the freshest follower, and let users read their own writes.
